extracted.intended_audience: members of the public, stakeholders, regulated entities, advocates, and agency staff who participate in or prepare federal rulemaking and public comments
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance on the phases of federal rulemaking and practical standards for submitting effective public comments (timing, substance, form, and where to find information). Useful for anyone preparing comments, petitions, or participating in notice-and-comment proceedings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pre-proposal identification of regulatory needs
rubrics_metrics.description: Agencies identify regulatory needs through statutes, court orders, petitions, or self-initiated review; pre-rule notices may include Requests for Information (RFI) or Advance Notices of Proposed Rulemaking (ANPRM).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use RFIs/ANPRMs to gather information early; understand that the agency may be in an exploratory stage before issuing a proposed rule.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proposed Rule (NPRM) required contents
rubrics_metrics.description: A proposed rule must be published in the Federal Register and include the legal authority, the substance and purpose of the proposed action, and an opportunity for public comment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or drafting an NPRM, check that the legal basis is cited, the rule text and its purpose are clear, and the mechanism for submitting comments is provided.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comment period length and timeliness
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment period typically 30–60 days; comments must be timely (submitted before the deadline).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plan submissions to meet the published deadline; missing the deadline can render a comment legally ineffective for influencing that rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive content of effective comments
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments should be substantive (not just preference statements); reference specific provisions; provide evidence, alternatives, or analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Concrete data, legal arguments, suggested regulatory text, and cost/benefit analysis strengthen a comment; vague or purely opinion-based remarks are less persuasive and less likely to affect agency decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comments as part of the administrative record and basis for judicial review
rubrics_metrics.description: Comments become part of the docket and form part of the basis for any judicial review of the agency action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because courts review the administrative record, thoughtful, documented comments can be critical to later litigation; ensure factual assertions are supported and clearly tied to specific rule provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paths for public participation
rubrics_metrics.description: Members of the public can submit written comments via Regulations.gov, participate in public hearings, request meetings with agency staff or OIRA, petition for new rules (5 USC § 553(e)), and challenge final rules in court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select the appropriate channel (written docket comment, hearing testimony, petition) depending on the goal; meetings with staff or OIRA may be appropriate for technical discussion but do not replace submitting comments to the docket.

rubrics_metrics.name: Final rule publication and preamble requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: After analyzing comments, agencies publish a final rule in the Federal Register that includes a preamble explaining responses to significant comments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble should demonstrate the agency considered important comments and explain how the final rule addresses them; omissions or inadequate responses can be grounds for challenge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effective date and Congressional Review Act considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Final rules typically have an effective date about 30 days after publication; substantively significant rules are subject to the Congressional Review Act.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Track effective dates for compliance planning; for major rules, monitor CRA procedures (e.g., Congressional disapproval windows) which can affect implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: OIRA review for significant rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Significant rules undergo OIRA review before publication.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use reginfo.gov and related tools to check OIRA review status; stakeholders seeking high-level input or interagency concerns should account for this review stage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Where to find authoritative rulemaking information
rubrics_metrics.description: Key resources include federalregister.gov (daily publication), regulations.gov (docket and comment portal), reginfo.gov (OIRA review status, Unified Agenda), USC Title 5 (APA text), and 1 CFR Part 51 (incorporation by reference).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consult these sources for official texts, docket materials, rulemaking schedules, statutory authority, and procedural rules governing submissions.
